title: Natural Hydrogen: Occurrence Evidence and the Limits of Industrial Claims
content: This critique assesses the evidence behind claims of industrial viability in natural hydrogen. It outlines what claims are backed by empirical fieldwork data, those based on analogous reasoning and those that are speculative. Four topics were investigated: 1) Scale of natural hydrogen resources, including the balance between production rates and exploitable resources; 2) Sustainability of natural hydrogen production based on geochemical processes of serpentinization and radiolysis; 3) Sensitivity of techno-economic analyses to assumptions in production rates and resource depletion; and maturity of technology within the natural hydrogen production process 4) Regulation in five countries (France, Australia, USA, Spain, Russia). Natural hydrogen resources and generating mechanisms are well understood. However, natural replenishment rates are many orders of magnitude lower than economically viable. Economic estimates strongly depend on unverified assumptions of steady-state production rates. Analogies to oil and gas systems are useful in exploration, however need modification when assessing resource volumes. Production bottlenecks include enhancing flow rates, processing poly-component gases at the wellhead and durability of hydraulically fractured rocks. For natural hydrogen to be legally recognised as a resource, licensing processes and resource estimation methods still need to be established. Consequently, natural hydrogen cannot yet be considered significant for energy security; verifiable claims of industrial viability require long-term reservoir testing and standardised resource estimations. Methodologically, this critical review demonstrates how generative AI can help academic literature searches, providing a systematic workflow to aid knowledge development within fast-moving research fields.
